title: Perfect Couple
statementMd:
Consider the function

$$ f(x, y) = x^3 y - x y^3 $$

For a positive integer $m$, two integers $x$ and $y$ are called an **$m$-perfect couple** if $f(x, y)$ is divisible by $m$.

You are given an array of $n$ integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ and $q$ queries. Each query consists of three integers $l$, $r$ and $m$.

For each query, find an $m$-perfect couple in the subarray $a_l, a_{l+1}, \dots, a_r$, or report that there is none. Formally, find two **distinct** indices $i$ and $j$ such that $l \le i, j \le r$ and $a_i$ and $a_j$ are an $m$-perfect couple, or report that no such pair of indices exists.

## Input

The first line of the input contains a single integer $t$ ($1 \le t \le 10^4$) — the number of test cases.

The first line of each test case contains two space-separated integers $n$ and $q$ ($2 \le n \le 10^6$, $1 \le q \le 10^5$) — the size of the array and the number of queries.

The second line of each test case contains $n$ space-separated integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ ($1 \le a_i \le 10^9$) — the elements of the array.

Each of the next $q$ lines contains three space-separated integers $l$, $r$ and $m$ ($1 \le l \lt r \le n$, $2 \le m \le 100$) — the description of a query.

It is guaranteed that the sum of $n$ over all test cases doesn't exceed $10^6$ and the sum of $q$ over all test cases doesn't exceed $10^5$.

## Output

For each query, output the answer in a line.

If an $m$-perfect couple exists in the subarray $a_l, a_{l+1}, \dots, a_r$, output two space-separated integers $i$ and $j$ ($l \le i, j \le r$, $i \ne j$) such that $a_i$ and $a_j$ are an $m$-perfect couple. If there are multiple answers, you may output any of them.

Otherwise, output $-1$.

## Note

In the first query of the first test case, $f(16, 15) = 7440$, $f(16, 11) = 23760$ and $f(15, 11) = 17160$. None of them is divisible by $7$.

In the second query of the first test case, $f(16, 9) = 25200 = 7 \times 3600$. So, $a_1$ and $a_4$ are a $7$-perfect couple.

In the third query of the first test case, $f(16, 15) = 7440$, $f(16, 11) = 23760$ and $f(15, 11) = 17160$ are all divisible by $5$. So, the pairs of indices $(1, 2)$, $(1, 3)$ and $(2, 3)$ are all correct answers.

In the fourth query of the first test case, $f(9, 4) = 2340$, which is divisible by $10$.

In the second test case, $f(15, 10) = 18750$, which is divisible by $6$, but not by $4$.
